RNC offers a useful implementation abstraction: proposal and auxiliary processes can be changed without deriving task-specific weight formulas, while established correctors arise as special cases.
The analytical reference process directly addresses an important finite-discretization instability. The density-estimation ablations support its value in the low-sample regime.

The experiments cover several nontrivial settings, including molecular annealing, multi-target ligand generation, learned energies, MCMC sampling, and free-energy estimation. Some gains are substantial, such as the ALDP energy TVD and recovery of useful MCMC energies.
The exposition is generally clear, and the extensive appendix provides derivations, pseudocode, limitations, and experimental details.
weaknesses: The conceptual core is largely a reformulation of Bayes/time-reversal identities and standard path-space importance weighting. Several advertised components are explicitly equivalent to prior estimators or regularizers, leaving the genuinely new technical contribution less sharp than the broad framing suggests.

Exact annealing and product correction assumes a perfect diffusion model, whereas the main experiments use learned models. The resulting bias is acknowledged but neither bounded nor measured, so the strongest practical claims lack a corresponding correctness guarantee. The CTMC generalization is also not evaluated empirically.

The main advantage over FKC depends on heuristically selecting ca and cb. These parameters are swept using target-quality metrics, with no held-out selection protocol or generally usable rule. On SBDD, the reported RNC-FKC differences are small relative to the very large variability and are not supported by significance tests.

The energy-training evaluation omits the closest Fokker-Planck-regularization baseline despite claiming equivalent but cheaper computation. There are also no sensitivity studies for the important regularization strength and time increment, or direct runtime/memory measurements supporting the efficiency claims.

The free-energy experiment is confounded and underspecified: the baseline trains only the energy network, while the RNE condition trains both energy and vector-field networks; the listed objective does not clearly include the vector-field loss, and its gradient treatment is unclear relative to the stop-gradient formulation in Eq. 23.

The convergence section states an O(Δt) rate but Proposition G.1 gives O(sqrt(Δt)); its proposition omits assumptions subsequently used in the proof, and some endpoint inequalities and continuous-time embedding steps require stronger justification. Numerous indexing, coefficient, and notation inconsistencies further reduce confidence in the formal claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code artifact is provided, many optimizer/training/MCMC details and random seeds are absent, and most results lack error bars or independent-run statistics. Overall, the work is promising and potentially useful, but these novelty, validation, and rigor issues place it slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

The divergence-free energy regularizer gives promising results across synthetic density recovery, ALDP sampling, and solvation free-energy estimation; the latter improves from 27.30 ± 0.45 to 29.28 ± 0.04 against a 29.43 reference.
The analytical-reference construction addresses an observed finite-discretization instability, and the appendix provides extensive derivations, ablations, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The novelty is difficult to isolate. The central identity is essentially Bayes' rule/time reversal on path space, while the principal applications are explicitly equivalent to or recover existing density estimators, FKC/TDS, and Fokker–Planck regularization. The paper does not establish clearly enough what is fundamentally new beyond unification, reference stabilization, and heuristic drift selection.

The advertised flexibility for annealing and model composition requires a perfect forward/reverse model pair. With learned scores, the resulting weights remain biased even with infinitely many particles; only the reward-tilting construction receives an exact imperfect-model treatment. There is no robustness bound or controlled study of score-model and discretization error.

The favorable RNC parameters are selected from task-specific sweeps using target-quality information, but no validation or deployable selection protocol is given. Table 1 lacks uncertainty estimates, while the RNC–FKC differences in Table 3 are small relative to the reported across-target dispersion and are unsupported by paired significance tests.

Important closest comparisons are missing: the energy regularizer is not empirically compared with the Fokker–Planck regularizer to which it is claimed equivalent, the density estimator is tested only with an exact score on a synthetic mixture, and the CTMC extension has no experiment. Runtime or memory measurements are also absent despite claims of negligible overhead.

Several theoretical statements need repair. Section G.3 announces an O(Δt) rate but Proposition G.1 states O(√Δt); its proof uses unstated Lipschitz, growth, and nondegeneracy assumptions and contains questionable bounding and indexing steps. The Fokker–Planck equivalence derivation has missing gradients and inconsistent powers of σ as written. Absolute-continuity conditions needed for applying the identities to an arbitrary process are not specified.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code is provided, and optimizer settings, learning rates, training durations for several models, seeds, model-selection procedures, and some data-generation details are missing. Numerous notation and editing errors further hinder verification.

strengths: The path-measure perspective provides a clean, useful unification of diffusion density estimation, SMC correction, and energy-based diffusion training, clarifying connections among several seemingly distinct prior methods.

RNC exposes meaningful flexibility in choosing sampling and auxiliary target dynamics. The ALDP annealing results show substantial TVD improvements over FKC, and the particle-scaling behavior is promising.

The divergence-free energy regularizer is simple and empirically effective across Gaussian mixtures, ALDP sampling, and solvation free-energy estimation while preserving the underlying diffusion model's sample quality.

The paper is ambitious, generally well organized, and supported by extensive appendices covering derivations, stabilization through an analytical reference process, limitations, and ESS/discretization behavior.
weaknesses: The foundational identity is essentially Bayes' rule/time reversal and is explicitly equivalent to existing Ito-density and Feynman-Kac constructions. The genuinely novel components—the flexible RNC design and energy regularizer—are not isolated against the strongest direct alternatives sufficiently well to establish a strong novelty claim.

Correctness for annealing, product, and CFG depends on a perfect time-reversal model and the continuous-time limit. The paper acknowledges that learned, discretized models yield biased weights and proves an exact imperfect-model result only for reward tilting, yet its main practical demonstrations emphasize annealing and product without quantifying this bias or convergence to the intended target.

The theoretical appendix contains notable consistency problems: Eq. 57 appears to invert the Gaussian-kernel ratio relative to Definition 2.1 and the subsequent derivation; Section G.3 announces an O(delta-t) rate while Proposition G.1 states O(sqrt(delta-t)); and parts of the convergence proof rely on underspecified regularity assumptions and questionable inequality steps. These issues undermine confidence in the claimed guarantees even if the core idea remains plausible.

The empirical evidence lacks statistical rigor. Key annealing results have no uncertainty estimates, the ligand-design differences are small relative to the reported cross-target variation, and no paired significance tests or robust multi-seed analyses are provided. The selection protocol for the swept parameters ca and cb is also unclear, creating a risk of test-set tuning.

Important comparisons and ablations are missing: there is no direct quality-and-cost comparison with Fokker-Planck regularization, no quantitative support for the claimed negligible overhead, limited density-estimation evaluation beyond an exact-score synthetic problem, and no comparison with dedicated multi-target molecular-design methods.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code is provided, and optimizer settings, learning rates, random seeds, several training budgets, MCMC configuration, and hyperparameter-selection procedures are absent. The broad CTMC and cross-modality claims also remain theoretical, with experiments concentrated on toy and molecular domains.
